article_title: Waterford Upstart
citation: Waterford Upstart program description. (2024). https://www.waterford.org/upstart/
title: Pair home-based adaptive learning software with family coaching and progress updates
description: The program pairs its software with structured family involvement: "Each family is also assigned a coach who provides onboarding, routine-building guidance, and ongoing check-ins throughout the program period." Families also receive "weekly progress updates, simple at-home learning tips, and access to a bilingual resource library (English/Spanish) to help reinforce skills offline," supporting consistent use in home settings.
requirements: Assignment of a coach to each family for onboarding and ongoing check-ins
Weekly progress updates and at-home learning tips for families
constraints: Designed for home implementation by families of young children, not classroom-only delivery
target_learners: Children in PreK–2 and their families
target_learning_goals: Consistent daily engagement with early literacy, math, and science lessons
examples: Families receive weekly progress updates and use a bilingual English/Spanish resource library to reinforce skills offline

article_title: TalkingPoints
citation: Academic Performance. (2024). TalkingPoints. https://talkingpoints.org
title: Family engagement tools should require no additional staffing or PD to be usable at scale
description: The article presents TalkingPoints as implementable without burdening schools: "No additional staffing required" and "There are no PD or training requirements for use." Support is instead embedded, with individual teacher accounts receiving in-app coaching and guidance, and school or district accounts able to access additional guided implementation and PD if desired.
requirements: In-app coaching and guidance must be built into teacher, school, and district accounts
constraints: Guided implementation and PD beyond in-app coaching are optional add-ons rather than included requirements
target_learning_goals: family-school partnerships supporting student outcomes
examples: Individual teacher accounts come with in-app coaching and guidance; school and district accounts can add guided implementation and PD

article_title: Teacher’s Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Act as a facilitator during collaboration: guide rather than direct, monitor groups, and intervene only when necessary
description: The primer's central during-collaboration principle is that collaborative learning works best when teachers act as facilitators. As the primer summarizes the research, "collaborative learning works best in classrooms where teachers act as facilitators: guiding rather than directing, empowering students, and using effective intervention techniques to support student learning." Teachers should stand back, let students interact, listen, and intervene when necessary — for example when a group is stalled, enmeshed in a misconception, or one student is dominating. Intervention is best done by asking questions to open up discussion. Teachers can use rubrics or checklists to monitor group climate, collaborative skills, and learning without feeling overwhelmed.
requirements: Well-structured tasks and clear expectations so students can sustain discussions without continuous teacher presence
constraints: The primer notes productive struggle is a key part of learning, but teachers must judge when struggle is too much and plan how to guide students toward the goal
target_learners: K-12 STEM students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: Sustaining meaningful peer discussion, self-regulation, and deeper content learning during group work
examples: The primer lists intervention situations including a stalled group, unanswerable questions, shared misconceptions, unresolvable disagreements, and a dominating student, with example teacher prompts for each
key_sources: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/6dc71c9f-b523-4c36-9da8-d98b364e17e0

article_title: Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students
citation: Alison Cheng, Bo Pei and Cheng Liu. (2025). Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 47–65. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8761
title: Incorporate fairness evaluation mechanisms into early at-risk student identification processes
description: The article recommends that at-risk identification practices, which traditionally emphasize early intervention and accuracy, should systematically evaluate fairness across demographic groups alongside predictive performance. It reports that "the findings also support the practice of incorporating fairness evaluation mechanisms into the process of identifying at-risk students", improving educator awareness of disparate impacts on underrepresented groups. This involves monitoring prediction rates and error types such as true positive and false negative rates across subgroups rather than pursuing overall accuracy alone.
requirements: Fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity, equal opportunity differences) computed alongside performance metrics at each identification stage
Examination of prediction rates across demographic subgroups
constraints: Fairness metric choice depends on educational context, stakeholder goals, and normative beliefs; different metrics can yield divergent conclusions
target_learners: High school students, particularly those from historically underrepresented groups
target_learning_goals: Equitable and timely identification of students needing academic support
examples: The study evaluated four fairness metrics across three course stages and three protected features, and applied ThresholdOptimizer post-processing to reduce bias while maintaining balanced accuracy
key_sources: Alison Cheng, Bo Pei and Cheng Liu. (2025). Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 47–65. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8761

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Build evaluation frameworks with faster metrics and role-specific data access to time contract decisions
description: The article identifies a timing misalignment: districts must make contract renewal decisions before reliable outcome data arrive, since state test results typically arrive in mid- to late summer after procurement cycles conclude. It recommends that districts "establish comprehensive evaluation frameworks that provide role-specific data access and identify faster, more reliable metrics beyond annual assessments to enable timely decision-making."
requirements: Usage dashboards for data-driven decisions
Adverse incident reporting systems
Early quality indicators including keyword detection at the input and output layers
constraints: Annual state assessment data arrives too late for procurement cycles, so faster interim metrics are needed
target_learning_goals: Judging AI-enabled edtech effectiveness and informing contract renewal decisions
examples: Recommended practices include usage dashboards, adverse incident reporting systems, and keyword detection at input and output layers

article_title: The Federal Role in Ending Teacher Shortages
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., DiNapoli, M., Jr., & Kini, T. (2023). The federal role in ending teacher shortages. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/649.892
title: Factory-model school heritage as the root cause of de-professionalized teaching conditions
description: The report argues that 'at the root of the crisis in teaching is the way teaching was conceptualized when our current school structures were designed a century ago' to accommodate compulsory mass education. Scientific managers applied Henry Ford's assembly-line model with 'more tightly prescribed curriculum, more teacher-proof texts, more extensive testing, and more regulations,' adopting age-grading and tracking as sorting mechanisms. Teachers were placed in 'egg-crate' classrooms with no scheduled time for planning, collaboration, or ongoing learning. The report states most schools 'still carry the marks of their industrial origins in the standardized structures, curriculum, and tracking systems; the design of the teaching job; and the lack of time and space for collaboration among teachers and personalization for students.'
requirements: Transformation of school structures toward strong relationships, personalization, and collaborative planning time, as in the report's sixth recommendation area
constraints: The report frames this as a historical-structural account of U.S. teaching conditions, noting today's schools are less regimented than they once were but retain industrial marks
target_learners: K–12 teachers and students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Understanding how school organizational design shapes teacher effectiveness, retention, and instructional quality
examples: The report contrasts U.S. conditions with high-achieving nations where teachers get 15 to 25 hours a week of planning and collaboration time, and notes only 47% of the U.S. education workforce are classroom teachers versus at least 70% in many other countries
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., DiNapoli, M., Jr., & Kini, T. (2023). The federal role in ending teacher shortages. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/649.892

article_title: Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, so Why Are University Faculties so White?
citation: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Faculty diversity pipeline programs (State Doctoral Scholars Program, STRIDE, California Pre-Doctoral Program)
description: The report profiles three initiatives it identifies as promising practices for diversifying the professoriate. The Southern Regional Education Board's State Doctoral Scholars Program provides "tailored faculty mentoring, networking, and financial support throughout their doctoral journey" and has helped more than 1,100 underrepresented students earn a Ph.D., with an 83% participant graduation rate. FIU's STRIDE offers mandatory best-practice workshops for hiring and promotion committees. The California Pre-Doctoral Program funds disadvantaged juniors, seniors, and graduate students for doctoral preparation, including GRE preparation and faculty mentoring.
requirements: Funding sources (e.g., NSF ADVANCE grants, state system funding) and institutional commitment to mentoring and financial support for underrepresented students
constraints: The report describes these as promising practices with output metrics, not as rigorously evaluated causal interventions
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students facing economic or educational disadvantages
target_learning_goals: earning a Ph.D. and entering faculty careers
reducing bias in faculty hiring
building the professoriate pipeline for students of color
examples: State Doctoral Scholars Program participants finish their Ph.D.s 2-5 years ahead of the national average; 80% of graduates are currently faculty, administrators, or postdoctoral researchers in the U.S.

article_title: AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques
citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: FastPerson multimodal video summarization system with chapter-level summary/full switching
description: FastPerson is a video-to-video summarization system that analyzes both visual and audio streams of lecture videos to generate condensed videos, using voice cloning to maintain the original speaker's voice and preserve continuity with the original lecture. Its interface "allows learners to seamlessly switch between summary and full versions on a chapter-by-chapter basis", letting learners select viewing granularity according to their comprehension level. In evaluation it cut viewing time by 53% on average without a significant quiz-score difference.
requirements: Multimodal analysis of visual (slides, board writing, gestures) and audio streams
Voice cloning technology to preserve the original speaker's voice
constraints: Existing text-only summarization loses the multimodal nature of video and breaks continuity with the original content, which this system is designed to avoid
target_learning_goals: Efficient grasping of core lecture content while retaining access to detail
examples: In the 40-participant evaluation, participants watched educational videos under summarized and normal playback conditions and completed comprehension quizzes

article_title: Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: A systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks
citation: AlSheikh MH, Zaini R, ALmulhem MA and Ahmad S (2026). Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: a systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks. Front. Educ. 11:1871468. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1871468
title: FACETS framework for describing AI innovations in education across six dimensions
description: The FACETS framework, introduced by Gordon et al. in BEME Guide No. 84, offers a structured approach to describe AI innovations in education across six dimensions: Form of AI, AI Use Case, Context, Education Focus, Technology, and SAMR. The review describes it as acting as a "compass" for reporting AI in education, combining details often reported separately into a single description. It was used as the coding schema in this review to classify each included study and enhance comparability across studies.
requirements: Authors must systematically address each facet (form, use case, context, education focus, technology, SAMR level) for the description to be complete and comparable
constraints: The review states FACETS may not directly assess educational outcomes
target_learning_goals: structured description and comparison of AI integration in teaching, learning, assessment, and curriculum design
examples: The review applied FACETS to 22 studies, summarizing each study in a row of Table 1 with facets and illustrative citations
key_sources: AlSheikh MH, Zaini R, ALmulhem MA and Ahmad S (2026). Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: a systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks. Front. Educ. 11:1871468. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1871468

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost
citation: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688
title: Guarantee fair-use incentives with monitoring mechanisms before expecting AI productivity gains
description: The paper argues that incentives for using AI are only legitimate when practitioners use AI to a similar degree, because heterogeneous use under relative evaluation produces inequality and erodes incentives to develop one's own skills. It claims: "the productivity impact of AI can be maximized if and only if incentives for fair use are strong, accompanied by monitoring mechanisms that detect misuse, given that the costs of unfair use are salient to practitioners." This factor is modeled as the incentive alignment component ωI of the organizational effectiveness modifier.
requirements: Homogeneity among practitioners in degree of AI use
Monitoring mechanisms that detect misuse
Costs of unfair use must be salient to practitioners
constraints: In high-stakes settings such as educational assessment, hiring, or safety-critical applications, verification procedures, human oversight, or usage restrictions may constrain the labor-saving benefits AI could otherwise provide
target_learning_goals: fair and appropriate use of AI tools
preserving incentives to develop one's own skills
examples: The paper notes adopting AI is the dominant strategy for individuals since it brings competitive results in shorter turn-around-time, but is effective only when all participants agree to a similar degree of use
key_sources: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688

article_title: Analysis and Prediction of At-Risk Students Using Machine Learning Algorithms
citation: Gheisari, S., & Salarian, H. (2024). Analysis and Prediction of At-Risk Students using Machine Learning Algorithms. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Analysis+and+Prediction+of+At-Risk+Students+using+Machine+Learning+Algorithms
title: Audit predictive retention models for fairness because underrepresented groups may be wrongly flagged as at-risk
description: The article treats fairness as a critical consideration in predictive retention modeling: training-data biases such as underrepresentation of certain nationalities, genders, or visa types may cause students to be inaccurately flagged as at-risk. It prescribes fairness audits as the mitigation: "To mitigate bias, future work should include fairness audits." The principle applies to any institutional deployment of dropout-prediction models.
requirements: Fairness audits of the trained model before or during institutional use
constraints: Risk arises specifically from underrepresentation of certain nationalities, genders, or visa types in training data
target_learners: higher education students, including international students of varied nationalities
target_learning_goals: equitable and accurate identification of at-risk students
examples: The study used a de-identified, anonymized SISTC dataset to meet ethical research standards

article_title: Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence
citation: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4
title: Argument-based validity and generalizability framing of AI-assigned scores as fallible observations with selective deferral
description: The article grounds AI-assisted grading in test theory and generalizability theory, treating AI-assigned points as "fallible observations with multiple error sources (items, raters/runs, tasks)" that can be estimated and, where appropriate, reduced through aggregation or design. For score interpretation it adopts Kane's argument-based validity perspective, requiring that claims about score meaning be supported by explicit warrants and evidence. The human-in-the-loop setup follows selective-prediction/deferral frameworks, in which the model grades confidently when reliable and defers uncertain cases to humans.
requirements: Explicit warrants and evidence must support claims about score meaning and decisions such as pass/fail cut scores
Error sources at item, rater/run, and task levels must be estimable for reliability analysis
constraints: The framework assumes run-to-run errors are approximately mean-zero and only weakly correlated across items
target_learners: higher-education students in large-enrollment STEM courses
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable automated scoring of open-ended handwritten assessment responses
examples: The study operationalized the framework with ICC(A,1)/ICC(A,k), repeatability Sw and RC, Kendall's W, and Lin's CCC, plus a two-parameter logistic IRT model defining risk as the absolute deviation between AI-assigned and expected scores
key_sources: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4

article_title: Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: A five-level family-school autonomy-support framework for children's responsible GenAI use, with evidence-tiered links
description: The review proposes a framework in which "Family-side and school-side inputs (Level 1) are hypothesized to act both directly and through a coordination layer (Level 2) on basic psychological need satisfaction (Level 3), which in turn supports moral and self-regulatory mediators (Level 4) and, through them, academic integrity and learning engagement (Level 5)." Links are graded into three evidence tiers: direct evidence in under-18s, indirect evidence from university samples, and theoretically specified but untested links. Table 1 operationalizes seven propositions (P1-P7) with family-side and school-side operationalizations and disconfirming results for each.
requirements: Comparable autonomy-support measures obtained from the same students in both settings to test the coordination layer
Behavioral rather than self-reported indices of responsible use
constraints: Because no reviewed study measured a family and a school input in the same participants, every link into and out of the coordination layer is Tier 3
The framework is a testable synthesis, not an established causal model
target_learners: children and adolescents using generative AI in learning
target_learning_goals: responsible, calibrated, and transparent GenAI use
learning engagement
academic integrity
examples: Table 1 states seven propositions P1-P7, each with family-side and school-side operationalizations, hypothesized processes, current evidence tier, and the result that would disconfirm it
key_sources: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217

article_title: Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: Three competing, falsifiable hypotheses for family-school coordination of autonomy support (additive, synergistic, compensatory)
description: Because family-side and school-side literatures rest on non-overlapping samples, the review states coordination as three competing hypotheses rather than an established effect. "H1 (additive): family and school autonomy support each predict responsible use, giving two main effects and no interaction. H2 (synergistic): the association between school autonomy support and responsible use is stronger where family autonomy support is high, giving a positive interaction." H3 (compensatory) holds that support in either setting is sufficient, giving a negative interaction. H2 is the version embedded in most current guidance and the one for which no evidence yet exists.
requirements: Discriminating the hypotheses requires comparable autonomy-support measures from the same students in both settings
A design powered for the interaction rather than for main effects
A factorial trial contrasting family-only, school-only, coordinated, and usual-practice guidance would be the strongest test
constraints: No equivalent test exists for GenAI; synergy should be treated as a hypothesis rather than an established effect
target_learning_goals: responsible GenAI use across home and school settings
examples: The review cites a meta-analysis of family-school partnership interventions improving children's social-emotional functioning in other domains, with efficacy moderated by which components are combined
key_sources: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217

article_title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
citation: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552
title: Fairness theatre: dashboard fairness metrics converge while groups' error burdens persist or worsen
description: Fairness theatre names the condition the article develops empirically: post-hoc adjustments that satisfy dashboard-level fairness metrics while the error burdens students and advisors actually experience stay the same or worsen. The article defines it as "post-hoc adjustments that make the metrics on an institution's dashboard look fair while the errors students and advisors actually live with stay the same or get worse." It stresses the pattern "isn't intentional deception" but is what procurement produces when fairness work is confined to vendor-exposed outputs. The concept was developed through evaluating six interventions under simulated procurement constraints.
requirements: A vendor-controlled predictive system whose design decisions are outside the institution's reach, with only calibrated outputs available for adjustment
constraints: The article develops the concept under simulated procurement constraints at a single Ontario college and reads findings as indicative of similar vendor-controlled settings, not settled facts about all of them
target_learners: Higher education students flagged or missed by early warning systems, including small and underrepresented demographic groups
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of scarce advising and retention-support resources across student groups
examples: The article's evaluation showed post-hoc adjustments can satisfy dashboard-level fairness metrics while leaving the distribution of error burdens intact or worse
key_sources: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552

article_title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
citation: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552
title: Fairness in procured AI as cooperative work negotiated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students
description: The article reframes post-hoc fairness in procured AI as a problem of cooperative work rather than a property of a model. It states that "fairness is not a property of a model but an outcome negotiated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students, and procurement contracts restrict the mutual visibility and control this negotiation requires." Vendors hold design knowledge, institutions hold knowledge of student populations and equity obligations, and the contract ensures neither party's knowledge reaches the other's decisions, leaving parties with starkly unequal power to accomplish fairness together.
requirements: Recognition that vendors, institutions, advisors, and students each hold part of what fairness requires, under a contract that currently blocks the needed alignment
constraints: Procurement contracts grant vendors authority over the model and leave institutions to govern only outputs, so the negotiation the framework requires is structurally restricted
target_learners: Students in institutions deploying vendor-supplied predictive systems, particularly those misrepresented in institutional data
target_learning_goals: Institutional fairness governance of algorithmic risk prediction in higher education
examples: The article examines the moment an institution, locked into a vendor-controlled predictive system, attempts to enact fairness on outputs it can observe but cannot meaningfully interrogate
key_sources: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552

article_title: Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support
citation: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205
title: FACTRIA: a framework of biasing factors for responsible institutional analytics interpretation
description: FACTRIA (Framework of Factors in the Analytical process and the data Context for Responsible Institutional Analytics) synthesizes fragmented knowledge on factors that hinder responsible interpretation of IA visualizations. As the article states, it is "a framework that organizes potential biasing factors across four areas: the analytics pipeline, institutional context, course-level characteristics, and demographics." It does not prescribe decisions but provides "a structured, evidence-informed scaffold" helping users surface implicit assumptions, question comparability, and recognize factors shaping interpretation. The framework is intended as flexible and extensible, with additional biasing factors to be incorporated as IA practices evolve.
requirements: Users must become familiar with the factors before interpretation; in the study participants read a framework summary before the task
constraints: The article states FACTRIA "remains a framework that may require adaptation across cases and institutional contexts" and does not prescribe how decisions should be made
target_learners: LMS and teaching-quality support staff in higher education
target_learning_goals: Responsible, bias-aware interpretation of institutional analytics dashboards
examples: The framework was encoded factor-by-factor into a chatbot and used to analyze four authentic IA cases on satisfaction, performance, LMS interaction, and LMS configuration diversity
key_sources: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205

article_title: Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support
citation: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205
title: FACTRIA-aware chatbot: a GenAI assistant with retrieval-augmented, framework-bound prompting for IA dashboards
description: A web-based, LLM-powered chatbot integrated into an IA dashboard that supports responsible interpretation of institutional analytics. Its interaction logic "uses a deterministic state machine to connect users' initial interpretations to the framework and emphasize relevant factors," then "cycles through F ACTRIA factors related to the visualization, providing prompts that guide reflection towards the visible data." Rather than offering interpretations or recommending decisions, it prompts users to reflect on data quality, assumptions, comparability, and other biasing factors via FACTRIA-aware retrieval-augmented generation.
requirements: Grounding in the FACTRIA framework through retrieval-augmented generation
Integration with a dashboard visualization so prompts reference the visible data
constraints: The article notes possible automation bias and over-reliance on chatbot guidance; some participants found prompts too generic and preferred more direct guidance
target_learners: Higher education stakeholders interpreting institutional analytics: professors, academic managers, and technical support staff
target_learning_goals: Factor-aware, responsible interpretation of institutional analytics visualizations
examples: In the study, each participant first interpreted a visualization without the chatbot and then the same visualization with FACTRIA-aware chatbot guidance across two of four authentic IA cases

article_title: Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing
citation: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914
title: Design educational AI writing tools to be fairness-aware, since biased assistants propagate gender stereotypes into student-authored text without users noticing
description: The article calls for "fairness-aware design in educational AI tools" after showing that a verifiably gender-biased LLM assistant transferred its bias into students' career-plan essays, suppressing female-target agency and raising gender-stereotypic occupational recommendations. Because biased-condition participants reported no awareness of influence, fairness cannot rely on user vigilance; the assistant's configuration itself must be checked. The article also shows a carefully configured neutral assistant may attenuate baseline stereotyping.
requirements: Verification that the assistant's prompts and outputs exhibit no measurable gender bias before deployment, as the article's validation phase did before the human study
constraints: Debiasing efforts targeting male over-representation would not fix this effect, which the authors say sits on the female side; transfer was demonstrated on a single open-source model (llama-3.3-70b-instruct), so generalization across model families remains untested
target_learners: undergraduate students using LLM writing assistance
target_learning_goals: career planning and written self-presentation free of gender-stereotypic framing
examples: The study's neutral LLM condition, configured to suggest careers based only on demonstrated experiences and skills, produced the lowest stereotype congruence rate of the three conditions

article_title: Knowledge Distillation for Automated AI Tutor Evaluation

title: FATE: a lightweight 8B-parameter LLM evaluator of AI tutors across four pedagogical dimensions

description: FCPS is the comparison condition in this study: it is "the same as the PF condition except that students received instructional facilitation throughout their lessons." Instructional facilitation provided throughout the lessons

citation: Klatte M, Bergström K and Lachmann T (2013) Does noise affect learning? A short review on noise effects on cognitive performance in children. Front. Psychol. 4:578. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00578
title: Design classrooms and school siting for favorable listening conditions, because effective listening is a linchpin of school learning
description: The review argues that children need more favorable listening conditions than adults for decoding and processing oral information, and that this has practical implications for the acoustical design of classrooms, "since effective listening is a linchpin of school learning". It extends this to school placement near airports and noise-abatement policy. Despite existing standards for ambient noise and reverberation, many classrooms still do not fit young listeners' needs.
requirements: Classroom ambient noise levels and reverberation meeting international and national standards developed in past decades
constraints: The review reports many classrooms still do not fit the needs of young listeners despite the standards
Chronic noise effects are usually small in magnitude and confounding variables were not always sufficiently controlled

target_learning_goals: speech perception and listening comprehension
reading and prereading skills
examples: Studies simulating classroom-like conditions of noise and reverberation reported severe impairments in children's listening performance

article_title: Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect
citation: Leppink, J., Broers, N. J., Imbos, T., van der Vleuten, C. P. M., & Berger, M. P. F. (2012). Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect. Higher Education, 63, 771-785. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-011-9476-1
title: Fading instructional guidance as prior knowledge develops: guided, semi-guided, then unguided problem-solving
description: The article proposes that, for a given subject matter and complexity level, educational practice could "strive for decreasing guidance as the course proceeds", moving through three phases: guided problem-solving with worked-out examples, semi-guided or self-guided problem-solving in which students integrate an indicated set of propositions into arguments, and unguided problem-solving in which learners select relevant premises themselves, closer to real statistical practice. The experiment grounds the first two phases: novices profited from worked-out examples while more knowledgeable students profited from formulating arguments.
requirements: Guidance level must be matched to students' current prior knowledge, increasing guidance for novices and reducing it as knowledge develops
constraints: Grounded in a single experiment on a small body of statistics subject matter (about one page of text) with a 50-minute exam; the unguided phase is proposed for future study rather than tested here
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of statistics
Argumentation integrating statistical propositions
examples: In the experiment, low prior knowledge students worked through worked-out examples of arguments (Box 3) while high prior knowledge students formulated arguments themselves (Box 2), and the article cites Aleven and Koedinger (2002) showing the more unguided approach can be effective in geometry

article_title: Influence of race/ethnicity and income on the link between adverse childhood experiences and child flourishing
citation: Goldstein, E., Topitzes, J., Miller-Cribbs, J. & Brown, R. L. (2021). Influence of race/ethnicity and income on the link between adverse childhood experiences and child flourishing. Pediatric Research. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-020-01188-6
title: Resilience-science framework: family resilience as a protective, partially mediating mechanism between childhood adversity and child flourishing
description: The article is informed by resilience science, which holds that identifying protective factors and processes is central to promoting child flourishing amid adversity. Family resilience is defined as "the ability of a family to withstand and rebound from disruptive life events" and is measured in the NSCH as a four-item composite (talking together, working together to solve problems, knowing strengths to draw on, staying hopeful). In the study's moderated-mediation model, this family-level construct operates as the mediator through which cumulative ACEs are partly transmitted to reduced flourishing in learning, task persistence, and self-regulation.
requirements: Requires measurement of family-level protective processes, operationalized here as the four-item NSCH family resilience composite requiring most-of-the-time or all-of-the-time responses on each indicator
constraints: The article states family resilience is only a partial mediator, so additional mediating influences are needed to explain the ACEs-flourishing association
Family resilience was found harder to muster for Black and Hispanic children facing adversity
target_learners: children ages 6-17 in the United States
target_learning_goals: interest and curiosity in learning new things
persistence in finishing tasks
emotional and behavioral self-regulation under challenge
examples: The study estimated family resilience as a latent mediator in a stacked-group probit moderated-mediation model using Mplus on 2016-17 NSCH data

article_title: Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46
title: Failure-fear-failure cycle: low math achievement from developmental dyscalculia gives rise to math anxiety, which further impedes achievement
description: The article proposes that developmental dyscalculia, an innate, heritable deficit in processing numerical information centered on intraparietal sulcus deficiencies, produces low math achievement from an early age, and that this low achievement leads to math anxiety rather than the reverse. The authors state that "low math achievement due to DD will lead to math anxiety", citing evidence that initial low achievement predicts later math anxiety, and frame the resulting dynamic as a cycle of "failure-fear-failure" that interventions could turn into "success-confidence-success".
requirements: The account presumes DD is a heritable, genetically-based condition with low numerical abilities present from a very early age
constraints: The authors state the causal direction is only a suggested hypothesis, since the current analysis cannot point directly to a causal connection between math anxiety and math achievement
target_learners: children with developmental dyscalculia aged 7 to 13
target_learning_goals: basic arithmetic fact retrieval and numerical processing
examples: The priming experiment showed DD children's arithmetic targets facilitated by negative and math primes, consistent with arithmetic facts being associated with negative emotions

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: The Faure-Delors heritage: an integrated humanistic vision framed by lifelong learning and four pillars of learning
description: The report identifies the two landmark UNESCO publications as key sources for policy makers, promoting 'an integrated and humanistic vision of education framed by the paradigm of lifelong learning and by the four pillars of learning to be, to know, to do, and to live together'. It treats this vision as a viable foundation for rethinking education, while noting it needs reappraisal under contemporary conditions. The four pillars are described as learning to live together, to know, to do, and to be.
requirements: The report states the vision requires 'a fresh reappraisal of this vision ... that takes into account contemporary conditions' to remain relevant
constraints: Translation of the lifelong learning paradigm into policy 'has remained more problematic in societies both in the North and South' because of the resource mobilisation it implies
target_learners: all children, youth and adults learning throughout life
target_learning_goals: holistic human development across knowing, doing, being and living together
examples: The report cites the 1996 Delors report's four pillars and the 1972 Faure report's introduction of lifelong learning as the forerunners of the current initiative

article_title: Components of executive control with advantages for bilingual children in two cultures
citation: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014
title: Faces task: a behavioral anti-saccade variant yielding three executive-control cost measures
description: The faces task is "a behavioral version of an anti-saccade task... developed by Bialystok, Craik, & Ryan (2006)" in which children respond to an asterisk appearing in one of two boxes flanking a schematic face, pressing the same side for green eyes and the opposite side for red eyes. Eyes look straight ahead or shift gaze toward a box, and trials appear in single-color or mixed blocks, producing straight-eye and gaze-shift tasks across blocked and mixed presentations. Sixteen blocks of 24 trials were administered, with counterbalanced orders and practice blocks, allowing calculation of suppression, inhibitory-control, and switching costs.
requirements: A computer with a response key on each side of the monitor and practice blocks of 8 trials before each task
constraints: Accuracy was near ceiling (97-98%) in 8-year-olds, so the task discriminates groups by response time rather than errors
target_learning_goals: Measuring response suppression, inhibitory control, and task-switching components of executive control
examples: Ninety 8-year-olds in three language groups completed the task with all conditions presented in one of eight counterbalanced orders.

article_title: Metacognitive emotion regulation: Children's awareness that changing thoughts and goals can alleviate negative emotions.
citation: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428
title: Assess young children's regulatory knowledge with familiar scenarios and multiple probe opportunities
description: The article argues that abstract, unfamiliar, single-probe tasks led prior research to underestimate 5- and 6-year-olds' metacognitive emotion regulation knowledge. When children were given familiar events and repeated opportunities to suggest strategies, the majority described metacognitive strategies. Assessments of young children's knowledge should therefore use familiar contexts and allow multiple responses before concluding a capability is absent.
requirements: Assessment tasks must use scenarios familiar to the child's own experience and provide repeated follow-up prompts
constraints: The article notes hypothetical tasks may not reflect what children would actually do in a real emotional situation
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of children's emotion regulation knowledge
examples: In Study 1, children heard four familiar narratives and received eight to sixteen prompts across stories; in Study 2, children recalled their own sad, angry, and scary events and described what they did to feel better.

article_title: Mindsets: A View From Two Eras
citation: Dweck, C. S., & Yeager, D. S. (2019). Mindsets: A View From Two Eras. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618804166
title: False growth mindset: educator practices that profess but fail to communicate a growth mindset
description: The article names "false growth mindset", a term coined by Susan Mackie, for practices of educators who profess a growth mindset but implement practices that fail to communicate it, sometimes doing the opposite. The core failure mode is that "many educators, it appeared, simply equated a growth mindset with effort", praising effort even when it was ineffective, which could leave students feeling incompetent; other forms include lecturing on mindset without changing classroom practices, and ignoring achievement differences so advanced students go unchallenged. The concept motivates the call for teacher curricula and mindset-supportive environments.
requirements: Educators need far more guidance than the authors initially provided, plus accurate understanding of what a growth mindset is and practices that embody it.
constraints: Focusing on effort alone, without good strategies, mentorship, and access to resources, can lead to blaming the victim when a person is not successful.
target_learners: K-12 and college students taught by educators implementing mindset practices
target_learning_goals: accurate growth-mindset communication
effective effort and strategy use
challenge seeking
examples: Educators put up posters or gave a lecture on growth mindset and then returned to business as usual, expecting students to do the rest.

article_title: Child and environmental risk factors predicting readiness for learning in children at high risk of dyslexia
citation: Dilnot, J., Hamilton, L., Maughan, B. and Snowling, M. (2017). Child and Environmental Risk Factors Predicting Readiness for Learning in Children at High-Risk of Dyslexia. Development & Psychopathology, 29(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/S0954579416000134
title: Family-risk of dyslexia as gene–environment interplay rather than a proxy for genetic risk
description: The article proposes that family-risk of dyslexia is "best conceptualized, not purely as a proxy for genetic risk, but as reflecting gene–environment interplay". Drawing on passive, evocative and active rGE mechanisms, it argues that parental genotype correlates with both the child's genetic risk and the environment parents provide, so familial effects on readiness operate through environmental channels such as a less rich home literacy environment. The study's finding that family-risk adds no variance once contextual risks are controlled supports this reframing.
requirements: A design that measures environmental and child-level risks alongside family-risk status so their unique contributions can be separated
constraints: The current design does not allow us to differentiate active/evocative from passive effects
It is unclear whether parental literacy should itself be considered an index of genetic risk rather than a measure of environmental variability
target_learners: preschool children at family-risk of dyslexia
target_learning_goals: reading readiness at school entry
attention and behaviour at school entry
examples: The study assessed family-risk via parental self-report on the Adult Reading Questionnaire, objective literacy testing, discrepancy criteria, or sibling diagnosis

article_title: The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic
citation: Camilla Gilmore, Sarah Keeble, Sophie Richardson, Lucy Cragg. (2015). The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic. ZDM Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-014-0659-y
title: Three-component taxonomy of arithmetic knowledge: factual, procedural and conceptual
description: The article organizes mathematics into components that cut across domains: "Factual knowledge comprises memorized number facts", procedural skill concerns "the accurate and efficient execution of operations" and can be thought of as 'knowing how', and conceptual understanding is "knowledge of the principles and relationships that underlie mathematics" or 'knowing why'. These components are not hierarchically ordered, individuals differ in their profiles across them, and they rely on differential sets of skills. The study used this taxonomy to pinpoint how inhibition relates to specific components rather than general tests.
requirements: Assessment instruments must separately capture each component rather than relying on general standardized mathematics tests
constraints: The article notes relationships among the components are complex and not hierarchically ordered
target_learning_goals: arithmetic factual knowledge
procedural skill
conceptual understanding
examples: The study administered a factual knowledge task (retrieval within 3 s), a procedural skills task (median RT for correct solutions) and a conceptual knowledge task (identifying relationships between problem pairs)

citation: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007
title: Computer-presented trajectories task on objects falling from stationary or moving carriers
description: The study used a computer-presented science task in which pairs discussed and predicted the trajectories objects follow when falling from stationary or moving carriers. The abstract describes a "computer-presented task that required them to discuss and predict the trajectories objects follow when they fall from stationary or moving carriers". It served as the collaborative activity linking group dialogue to post-test measures of individual understanding.
requirements: Pairs of students must discuss and predict object trajectories together
target_learning_goals: predicting the trajectories of falling objects (physical science reasoning)
examples: Forty-six pairs of students aged between 10 and 22 years worked on the task in the reported study

article_title: Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sten Ludvigsen, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl. (2017). Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12:215–220. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9265-7
title: Design scaffolding with attention to over-scripting risk and plan for fading scripting support over time
description: The editorial highlights integration of multiple scaffolds as carrying a danger of over-scripting or script interference, and notes that fading of scripts offers promise for reducing scripting over time and thus potentially avoiding over-scripting. Fading remains associated with many open and difficult questions, but the principle is that scaffold intensity should be designed to be reduced rather than fixed.
requirements: Knowledge of student-level variables such as prior knowledge and working-memory capacity that moderate scaffolding effectiveness
constraints: Fading is a topic with few landmark studies so far and many open and difficult questions; the Matthew Effect means scaffolding may benefit high-prior-knowledge students more than the low-prior-knowledge students it targets
target_learning_goals: mathematical argumentation skills
collaborative argumentation
examples: The editorial points to potential dynamic fading that responds in real time to differences in argumentation patterns based on automated analysis, and to fading connected to different appropriation trajectories for students

article_title: Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn
citation: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7
title: Design drawing support to facilitate integration of verbal and pictorial models, not merely to reduce load or increase generative activity
description: When students draw to learn, support should specifically guide them to integrate their verbal and pictorial models with prior knowledge into a coherent mental model. The article concludes that "it seems essential to help students make sense by integrating the verbal and pictorial models into a coherent mental model that can consistently be stored in long-term memory." Support that only keeps learners active or eases drawing demands did not reliably help.
requirements: Support must prompt learners to build referential connections between their verbal and pictorial models, e.g., explaining while drawing or comparing their drawing with a provided illustration
constraints: Evidence covers comprehension of science content learned from text with hand drawing; transfer moderator analysis was not conducted (k = 7 effect sizes, below the k = 10 rule of thumb)
target_learners: school, high-school, and undergraduate students in STEM learning contexts
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension of complex science content through drawing-to-learn activities
examples: In the meta-analysis, support such as explaining while drawing, viewing a teacher drawing while checking one's own drawing, and revising drawings by inspecting a provided illustration was coded as facilitating integration and showed g = 0.35

article_title: Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study
citation: Li Zhao, Junjie Peng, Shiqi Ke, Kang Lee. (2024). Effectiveness of Unproctored vs. Teacher-Proctored Exams in Reducing Students’ Cheating: A Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Field Experimental Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09965-z
title: Fake Question Paradigm for objective measurement of exam cheating
description: The Fake Question Paradigm is an objective behavioral measure of cheating in real exams. "This paradigm involved adding researcher-prepared fill-in-the-blank target questions to the exam questions prepared by the professors"; the target questions appear course-related but test fictional concepts with fake answers unavailable online or in books. The answer key is posted to the class portal after the exam starts, so "any correct answer would indicate cheating and the number of correct answers would measure the extent of cheating." Fill-in-the-blank format minimizes guessing, and different target questions per section prevent answer sharing.
requirements: Target questions must test fictional concepts whose answers do not exist on the internet or in books, verified by pilot testing and internet searches
The answer key must be posted online during the exam while students are told not to check it, so correct target answers can only arise from cheating
constraints: Requires a context where posting answer keys to a class portal during exams is routine practice
Students must put away electronic devices before the exam starts so portal access constitutes cheating
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of academic dishonesty in actual course exams
examples: In Study 1, five fill-in-the-blank target questions about fictional concepts (e.g., a fake tenth force in Western psychology) were added to a 17-question professor-prepared midterm, after a pilot study (N = 64) verified students could not answer them correctly

article_title: Joy is reciprocally transmitted between teachers and students: Evidence on facial mimicry in the classroom
citation: Frenzel, A. C., Dindar, M., Pekrun, R., Reck, C., & Marx, A. K. G. (2024). Joy is reciprocally transmitted between teachers and students: Evidence on facial mimicry in the classroom. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101896. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101896
title: Facial mimicry as a micro-level bottom-up mechanism driving macro-level teacher–student emotional contagion
description: The article proposes that macro-level covariation between teachers' and students' self-reported habitual joy experiences is fueled, in a bottom-up fashion, by micro-level covariation: repeated instances of joint joy experiences during instruction. Facial mimicry is positioned as a key mechanism, defined as one person facially expressing their emotional state which is "mirrored, or imitated, by their interaction partner within seconds". The framework draws on the "social glue" function of emotional mimicry, which fosters affiliation between interaction partners, and proposes that persistent micro-level mimicry processes lead habitual emotional experiences in the joint context to converge over time.
requirements: Both interaction partners must engage in a joint activity during which they can mimic each other's facial expressions for substantial proportions of their interaction.
constraints: The article notes the degree of emotional mimicry depends on individual, contextual, and relational factors such as prior affiliation, group membership, and attitudes, and occurs less in competitive or hostile settings.
target_learning_goals: positive emotional experiences during instruction
teacher-student relational and emotional convergence
examples: The study operationalized the mechanism using cross-recurrence quantification analysis on frame-by-frame facial joy expression time series from 69 instructor–student dyads, identifying a critical lag window of -54 to +85 lags.

description: On the genetic view, the child's mind and every idea in it go through a process of development, and attempts to quickly mold the mind or a single idea into mature form are 'sure to fail'. article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Fast motions are essentially different from slow motions in both industrial and intellectual work.
description: Bird's central thesis, stated in her conclusion, is that "Fast motions are essentially different from slow motions not only in industrial but in intellectual work." Drawing on Gilbreth's observation that a bricklayer used different motions when working slowly than when working rapidly due to different muscle tension, and on her own addition experiments showing more errors and distractions under slow work, she argues slow work follows a devious path cluttered with irrelevant bonds.
requirements: The distinction rests on the assumption that rapid, properly focalized practice establishes habits that eliminate superfluous intermediate performances.
constraints: Bird notes further investigation might show decreased efficiency even more marked than the reduction of accuracy observed.
target_learning_goals: efficient skill automatization
speed with accuracy
examples: Bird describes how in slow addition a person may revert to wasteful childhood habits such as counting on fingers, lip movement, and vocalization.

article_title: Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword
citation: Lea Nobbe, Jasmin Breitwieser, Daniel Biedermann & Garvin Brod. (2024). Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword. npj Science of Learning 9:40. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00253-7
title: Design study reminders to fade out and to build habits through learner-owned cues and implementation intentions rather than dependence on prompts
description: The article argues that because reminders can create reliance, interventions promoting self-regulated learning should aim for studying that persists without prompts: "Ideally, then, reminders should fade out over time, while the frequency of studying should remain the same." It recommends anchoring studying to recurring situations in students' daily lives, using plans and implementation intentions that let learners express their own timing preferences, and designing reminders "when helping to form a habit through establishing easily identi ﬁable study cues in students' daily lives rather than in their phones."
requirements: Reminders must align with students' intentions and be implemented together with them, per the article's discussion of nudging in education.
constraints: The article states its findings come from German lower secondary students aged 10–12 studying vocabulary, and that generalization to older students and other learning strategies is unclear.
target_learning_goals: distributed practice in self-study
self-regulated vocabulary learning
examples: In the study, the Reminder Group saw a screen reminding them of a video on distributed practice on 16 of 36 days, pseudorandomly assigned, while the Control Group watched the video only.

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep
citation: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2
title: Face-name TMR experimental protocol: two music-associated classes, nap cueing, and interference learning
description: A laboratory procedure in which participants learned 80 face-name pairs (40 per class, ostensibly Japanese History and Latin-American History classes), each class with a distinctive instrumental music track. Learning combined face viewing with spoken and written names, recall training with feedback, and visualization practice. Presleep tests assessed recognition (230 faces: old, rotated, new) and name recall; a mean 59-minute nap followed with manual TMR cueing during N3; interference learning of 20 new pairs preceded postsleep tests.
requirements: EEG recording to detect N3 sleep and pause cueing on transitions to other stages or wake
Spoken-name cue intensity manually controlled at 45–50 dB peak, the highest volume possible without causing arousal
constraints: Due to a technical error, the study could not test whether TMR effects differed for spoken-name-plus-music cues versus music-only cues within the cued class

target_learning_goals: face recognition and name recall for newly learned people
examples: Each to-be-learned person was presented twice, face shown once in quarter-right and once in quarter-left orientation, with a one-sentence biographical fact

citation: Peña, M., Vásquez-Venegas, C., Cortés, P., Pittaluga, E., Herrera, M., Pino, E. J., Escobar, R. G., Dehaene-Lambertz, G., & Guevara, P. (2024). A brief tablet-based intervention benefits linguistic and communicative abilities in toddlers and preschoolers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00249-3
title: Fast mapping as a word-learning process for designing early vocabulary interventions
description: Fast mapping is described as "a word-learning process that creates an initial association between a new word and its meaning". The authors adopted it to design their game because previous studies showed toddlers and preschoolers succeed in this task in the short and long term, and because fast-mapping ability is positively associated with concurrent and subsequent language development in late-talking, typically developing, and atypically developing children. The game operationalizes fast mapping by training each word-object association only once across sessions.

constraints: In the authors' pilot, children successfully learned uncommon word-object associations but struggled with pseudoword-object associations

Pre-reading letter-sound associations

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Familial Control Method: parental traits as covariates proxy-controlling for genetic transmission in rearing-environment studies
description: The Familial Control Method is defined as "Using a measure of the same trait in the parent as the child as a covariate in models estimating the effect of the rearing environment"; the covariate "serves as a proxy control for the genetic transmission effect". The authors advise assessing the trait in both parents, because the child shares all their genes with both parents but only 50% with one. It is designed for traits transmitted mostly through genes, like reading ability, and is currently the most feasible proxy genetic control for most behavioral researchers, requiring neither twin/adoption samples nor DNA.
requirements: Both parents should be assessed to best tag the child's genetic liability
The trait measured in parents should be the same or highly similar to the child's trait, reasonably measurement invariant and genetically stable across cohorts and lifespan
constraints: If parent–child resemblance also reflects environmental transmission, the method can be too conservative, removing some true environmental variance
Correlations are attenuated by measurement error; structural equation modeling with multiple indicators reduces this
target_learners: children and their parents in family-based educational research
target_learning_goals: testing direct environmental effects (e.g., home literacy/numeracy environments) on children's academic outcomes free of genetic confounding
examples: Van Bergen et al. used step-wise regression with parents' reading ability as covariates for home-literacy indicators; Hart et al. applied it to the home numeracy environment and children's math ability
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: Debiasing Education Algorithms
citation: Jamiu Adekunle Idowu. (2024). Debiasing Education Algorithms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00389-4
title: Evaluate the fairness of data and features before algorithmic fairness
description: The review recommends that developers assess the fairness of data and features used in educational algorithms before addressing algorithmic fairness itself, to "prevent algorithms from receiving discriminatory inputs". Biased data and features reflect historical prejudices, demographic inequalities, and cultural stereotypes, and feature unfairness is difficult to detect later in model implementation. The review notes limited work has addressed this aspect despite its importance.
requirements: Evaluation of distribution and hardness bias in datasets, and extraction of fairer features with feature-fairness evaluation, before model training
constraints: The review notes limited work has been done in evaluating bias in data and feature engineering
target_learners: students in educational settings whose data feeds predictive algorithms
target_learning_goals: preventing discriminatory inputs to dropout, performance, and classification models
examples: S2 found all three datasets (Moodle, KDDCUP 2015, OULA) exhibited distribution and hardness bias, and class-balancing techniques reduced this bias

citation: Goldberg, B., Amburn, C., Ragusa, C., & Chen, D. (2018). Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:194–224. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0155-y
title: Instrumented FATS M100 marksmanship simulator with BioHarness breathing sensor and GIFT data logging
description: The data-collection apparatus combines Meggitt's FATS M100 Advanced Reality Simulator—a simulated M4 carbine with embedded sensors—with a Zephyr BioHarness BT wireless breathing strap, all logged through GIFT on a synced timestamp. The weapon was "designed with embedded sensors, including: point of aim through an infrared laser mounted in the barrel at a 6 Hz sampling rate, a trigger sensor that measures displacement during the execution of a shot, butt-stock pressure, and the weapon's cant angle". A custom GIFT Gateway plug-in received simulator data over TCP, and a GIFT plug-in received BioHarness data wirelessly via Bluetooth at approximately 18 Hz.
requirements: Time-synced logging across sensor channels via GIFT for post-hoc merging
Mechanical and digital zeroing of the weapon before data collection
constraints: Weapon cant and butt-stock pressure were not analyzed in this work
Recoil was approximately 70% of a real weapon's intensity
Automatic dispersion and wind effects were disabled

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: FATE in AIEd conceptualized as four interwoven, inseparable dimensions
description: The article defines FATE in AIEd as four interwoven dimensions: fairness attends to discrimination based on contextual and temporal student characteristics; accountability provides mechanisms for teacher knowhow and institutional resources; transparency discloses design rationale to practitioners; and ethics keeps "values of fairness, local voice, and agency in view". The authors state the dimensions are "interwoven and inseparable from one other", so a fairness issue entails transparency, ethics, or accountability problems.
requirements: Design, development, and implementation processes must address all four dimensions together rather than in isolation
constraints: The conceptualization was derived from literature within AI and AIEd communities, not empirically tested in this article
target_learning_goals: Fair and equitable algorithmic decision-making in educational technology

article_title: Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be!
citation: Alexandron, G., Yoo, L. Y., Ruipérez-Valiente, J. A., Lee, S., & Pritchard, D. E. (2019). Are MOOC Learning Analytics Results Trustworthy? With Fake Learners, They Might Not Be! International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 29, 484–506. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00183-1
title: Fake-learner detection algorithms for CUMA and unauthorized collaboration in MOOCs.
description: The article uses dedicated algorithms to identify two types of fake learners: "Copying Using Multiple Accounts (CUMA)", where a master account receives credit while harvesting accounts collect correct answers, and unauthorized "Collaborators" who submit assignments together, detected using dissimilarity metrics on submission timing. In the 8.MReVx course, the CUMA algorithm detects 65 master accounts out of 478 certificate earners (a lower bound), and the collaborator algorithm identifies 20 (~4%) of certificate earners.
requirements: Detection requires sophisticated algorithms that are currently not available as off-the-shelf tools for cleaning data.
constraints: The CUMA algorithm is designed to provide a lower bound on the true number of master accounts, and the algorithms detect only a subset of fake learners; other fake learning methods may exist.
target_learning_goals: identifying non-learning behavior that biases analytics of learning in MOOCs
examples: In the MITx 8.MReVx Summer 2014 course, the algorithms identified 65 CUMA master accounts and 20 collaborators among certificate earners, with 11 accounts using both methods.

citation: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). Learning to Overcome Cultural Conflict through Engaging with Intelligent Agents in Synthetic Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0031-y
title: FAtiMA cognitive appraisal agent architecture with cultural Theory of Mind
description: FAtiMA (Fearnot AffecTIve Mind Architecture) is a cognitive appraisal architecture in which events are assessed in relation to agent goals and generate an affective outcome, used in reactive action-tendency rules and a deliberative planning system generating coping behaviours based on hope and fear. For MIXER it was extended with a 1-level Theory of Mind consisting of a collection of Models of Others forming a recursive hierarchical tree, encoding equivalents to Baron-Cohen's Eye-Direction Detection and Shared-Attention Mechanism capabilities. Making the utility of goals depend on cultural values establishes a link between culture and behaviour, so agents' appraisal and action generation are culturally dependent.

constraints: A 1-level Theory of Mind is modelled, with Models of Others recursing one level
target_learning_goals: experiencing believable intercultural conflict between synthetic cultures
examples: In MIXER, agents choose options to maximise expected utility, e.g. to not be 'killed' out of the Werewolves game

citation: Falloon, G., & Jones, M. (2026). Human–machine knowledge building: reconceptualising knowledge building partnerships in the age of artificial intelligence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10605-2
title: Three-zone model for human–GenAI knowledge building partnerships
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of three overlapping Zones—Reckoning, Collaboration and Judgement—aligned with Krathwohl's revision of Bloom's cognitive domain, describing how humans and GenAI might partner in collaborative knowledge construction. It states the model identifies "a possible 'division of labour' within and across Zones" while arguing "the primacy of innately human capabilities operating in the Judgement Zone". The zones interact iteratively rather than hierarchically, with circular arrows between the Collaboration and Judgement zones representing continuous human evaluation of AI-human outputs.

constraints: The article states the model is not intended as a hierarchy or linear process, and that zone boundaries and activities may change as the technology evolves

target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building with GenAI
reasoned judgement and ethical decision-making about AI-generated information

citation: Curtis J. Bonk, David A. Wiley. (2020). Preface: Reflections on the waves of emerging learning technologies. Education Tech Research Dev 68:1595–1612. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09809-x
title: Fall in love with the problem, not the technology: anchor learning technology research in problems learners face

citation: Yanjun Pan, Elizabeth L. Adams, Leanne R. Ketterlin-Geller, Eric C. Larson, Corey Clark. (2024). Enhancing middle school students' computational thinking competency through game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10400-x

description: Factory Craft is a "first person, three-dimensional, multi-level role-player game that aims to enhance CT competency for middle school students."
