article_title: Characteristics of laparoscopic and open hernia repair simulation models: a systematic review.
citation: Pelly T., Vance-Daniel J., Linder C. (2021). Characteristics of laparoscopic and open hernia repair simulation models: a systematic review. Hernia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8251686/
title: Three-domain validity framework for evaluating surgical simulation models
description: The review applies a three-domain validity framework to classify hernia repair simulation models. As the review defines it, "Face validity was defined as the physical realism of the simulator", construct validity as the ability to differentiate performance by experience level, and content validity as expert-judged suitability as a teaching modality. Each of the 27 included models is tabulated against these three domains plus educational impact and skill transfer.
requirements: Developers must assess models against the defined validity domains after design and implementation to establish educational value
constraints: The review notes the literature's validity definitions are nebulous and vary from those applied in this review, with a need for more consensus

target_learning_goals: technical competence in hernia repair procedures
examples: The review classified all 27 included models by face, construct and content validity, educational impact and transfer of skills to the operating theatre

article_title: Evaluation of simulation models in neurosurgical training according to face, content, and construct validity: a systematic review.
citation: Chawla Shreya, Devi Sharmila, Calvachi Paola, Gormley William B., Rueda-Esteban Roberto. (2022). Evaluation of simulation models in neurosurgical training according to face, content, and construct validity: a systematic review. Acta Neurochirurgica. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00701-021-05003-x
title: Face, content, and construct validity framework for evaluating simulation models as educational tools
description: The review organises simulator evaluation around three validity types: "Face validity examines the realism of a simulator and difficulty level similarity in comparison to real training tasks, whilst content validity assesses the model's effectiveness during a specific skill training to improve participants' techniques". Construct validity is the objective method "that considers the ability of a simulator to differentiate levels of skill competence". The review applies this framework to cadaver, animal/placenta, synthetic, and VR models across four skull-base procedures, and names predictive validity as an ultimate, unassessed fourth type.
requirements: Subjective validity types (face and content) are evaluated by questionnaires; construct validity requires distinguishing participants at different levels of experience and expertise.
constraints: The review states there is no consensus on the gold standard to assess medical and surgical education outcomes, and predictive validity assessment is logistically impractical due to long-term follow-up requirements.
target_learning_goals: validating simulation-based training tools for surgical skill acquisition
examples: The review used this framework to synthesise 18 studies, finding all reported face validity, 11 content validity, and 6 construct validity.

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Ten-topic-area taxonomy of family medicine education research
description: The review organizes family medicine education research into a set of topic areas identified through scoping review of 624 articles. The authors state: "The following research topic areas were identified: continuing education, curriculum development, undergraduate education, teaching methods, assessment techniques, selection of entrants, non-clinical skills, professional and faculty development, clinical decision-making and resident well-being." This taxonomy maps the field's substantive foci and serves as a benchmark for assessing future changes in educational scholarship.

constraints: Derived from literature published 2002 to 2012 in English only; commentaries and purely descriptive curriculum papers excluded
target_learning_goals: mapping the substantive topic areas of family medicine education research

article_title: Technology Integration and the Effect on Mathematics Fact Fluency in the Middle East
citation: Letwinsky, K. M., & Berry, M. D. (2017). Technology Integration and the Effect on Mathematics Fact Fluency in the Middle East. Journal of International Education and Leadership, 7(1). http://www.jielusa.org/
title: Fact fluency as a speed-and-accuracy construct attained through Baroody's three developmental stages
description: The article frames fact fluency as a construct commonly defined by speed and accuracy, drawing on Baroody's definition of fluency as "the efficient, appropriate, and flexible application of single digit calculation skills". It distinguishes automaticity as execution with minimal cognitive effort, and presents Baroody's three stages: modelling and/or counting; deriving answers using reasoning strategies; achieving mastery by efficiently producing answers.
requirements: Retention of facts requires the explicit development of reasoning strategies, which helps students master facts and regenerate a forgotten fact.
constraints: Traditional rote drill and timed testing force students to attempt to move from stage 1 directly to stage 3, which the article reports as problematic for retention.
target_learners: elementary students learning basic number combinations
target_learning_goals: mathematical fact fluency, automaticity, and number sense
examples: The study operationalized fluency as completion time and accuracy on 30-problem multiplication tests, and curriculum frameworks such as CCSM and IB PYP include automatic recall expectations.

article_title: Effectiveness of Fathom on Statistical Reasoning among Form Four Students
citation: Nanteni Ganesan & Leong Kwan Eu. (2018). Effectiveness of Fathom on Statistical Reasoning among Form Four Students. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 6(4). http://mojes.um.edu.my/
title: Fathom dynamic data software as a pedagogical tool for statistical concept development
description: Fathom is dynamic statistics software developed by chief designer Bill Finzer in the mid-1990s, targeting secondary and higher education students. The article stresses that it "is a pedagogical tool designed for concept development (Finzer, 2001), rather than software designed for professional data analysis". Its design drew on research about how students learn statistical concepts, and its dynamic nature and friendly interface let students manipulate a statistical environment, produce graphs, and visualize multiple representations of data and observe the effects of their own actions.
requirements: Used within lessons that let students explore and analyse data and discuss their reasoning, as in the experimental condition of this study.
constraints: The article's effectiveness evidence comes from one eight-week quasi-experiment with 72 Form Four students in a private Selangor school; the authors recommend testing on a larger sample with a longer intervention.
target_learning_goals: Statistical thinking, graph construction and interpretation, and statistical reasoning about data
examples: In this study the experimental group used Fathom to perform basic computations, giving students chances to access and explore a variety of information on the graphs.

article_title: Formative Assessment as a Tool to Enhance the Development of Inquiry Skills in Science Education

title: Database of formative assessment classroom techniques (FACTs) for science subjects
description: The intervention element is a prepared database of Formative Assessment Classroom Techniques (FACTs) for chemistry, biology, physics, mathematics and informatics, created by subject-didactics experts and given to participating teachers. The article notes that "Using FACTs is not time consuming, yet it can provide the teacher with a good overview and feedback on the lessons and at the same time, students get feedback on their own learning." Teachers selected FACTs at their own discretion, using at least three subjects with FACTs at least once a week; ten FACT types were logged with average uses per student ranging from .5 (K-W-L chart) to 2 (true/false statements, task cards).

FACTs must address the content of the respective lesson

self-assessment and metacognition
scientific thinking
examples: During the 5-month implementation, teachers and didactics experts met three times to share experience; every FACT addressed the content of the respective lesson

description: The article recommends building FA capacity at the level of teacher education and educational policy, not only in classrooms. Investment in professional development, mentoring and peer-support
Ready-made FACTs databases and continual methodological guidance
constraints: The article notes these requirements are not addressed systematically in Slovakia; current efforts are partial, via VEGA and KEGA projects and methodology-centre training

inquiry skills development
examples: The authors' own VEGA and KEGA projects build teacher materials, digital FACT collections, methodological materials, and contact and online teacher education focused on new assessment forms

family support for social adjustment

article_title: Examining Family-School Engagement in a Randomized Controlled Trial of the Family Check-Up
citation: Garbacz, S. A., Stormshak, E. A., McIntyre, L. L., & Kosty, D. (2019). Examining family-school engagement in a randomized controlled trial of the family check-up. School Psychology, 34, 433–443. https://doi.org/10.1037/spq0000284
title: Family Check-Up (FCU) adapted as a school-based, family-centered intervention for kindergarten
description: The Family Check-Up is described as "an ecological, school-based, family-centered intervention" that "includes an initial interview and ecological assessment, followed by a feedback session", with motivational interviewing embedded throughout to promote motivation to change. The kindergarten adaptation delivered a home visit with videotaped assessment and a feedback session in the home, integrated reading and math assessments, teacher reports, and parent–child observations, and followed a tiered service delivery model offering universal, selected, and indicated support tailored to family needs and risk.
requirements: Therapists trained in the FCU protocol, motivational interviewing, and academic supports, with COACH fidelity ratings within the acceptable range before independent delivery
constraints: The article notes the FCU was previously tested in early childhood and middle school; the kindergarten adaptation had not been examined before this study
target_learners: kindergarten children and their families in Title I elementary schools
target_learning_goals: parenting skills, home-to-school planning, family-school communication, and academic and behavior support at home and school

article_title: Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments?
citation: Ho, P. V. P., Phung, L. T. K., Oanh, T. T. T., & Giao, N. Q. (2020). Should Peer E-Comments Replace Traditional Peer Comments? International Journal of Instruction, 13(1), 295-314. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13120a
title: Facebook group as a platform for asynchronous peer e-comments on writing drafts
description: A closed Facebook group served as the asynchronous platform through which experimental-group students exchanged peer comments on each other's drafts. The teacher "created a Facebook group and ensured all participants in the experimental group joined the Facebook group"; students posted drafts, commented below posts, and received teacher comments typed in the Comment Section. The article contrasts this with the control group's face-to-face paper-and-pen exchange, noting the platform removes the need for in-person meetings.

Students must be trained to give peer comments using guidelines
constraints: Requires students to have access to the Internet and computers
target_learners: non-English-major university freshmen at pre-intermediate (A2 CEFR) level
target_learning_goals: improving L2 email-writing quality
examples: Students posted first and second drafts on the Facebook group across three two-week writing cycles, with teacher comments typed in the Comment Section below each post

citation: Ngo, C. M. & Trinh, L. Q. (2011). description: Each process-approach lesson moved students "from modeling to collaborative practice and then to individual practice", ensuring clear input and consolidation. constraints: Interviewed students who lacked linguistic competence struggled to suggest corrections beyond ticking the checklist
target_learners: Grade-10 EFL students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: Generating and organizing ideas, drafting, peer evaluation, and revision in English writing
examples: The experimental group worked through eight such lessons on the first eight units of English for Grade 10 over sixteen weeks

title: Family and Friends 2 MultiRom computer-based grammar activities

No home access to the MultiRom was permitted in the study

examples: Experimental groups used the software during 12 treatment sessions, one group for twice as long as the other

citation: Vahid Rafieyan, Maryam Sharafi-Nejad, Zahra Khavari, Lin Siew Eng & Abdul Rashid Mohamed. (2014). Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration. English Language Teaching, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n2p11

A fixed weekly interaction hour convenient to both sides
Researcher-designed and supervised group structure

The same 14 topics instructed by the educator in both groups

writing attitude
writing anxiety
writing self-efficacy

listening and speaking
practical interaction in English

guidance to lexicographic databases such as WordNet

article_title: The Impact of Musical Mnemonic on Vocabulary Recalling of Iranian Young Learners

vocabulary comprehension
examples: In the study, the experimental group learned 14 coursebook words sung to "Let It Go" across sessions while the control heard the same list spoken at one word per second

article_title: The Effect of Critical Discourse-Based Instruction on Iranian English Major Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Javadi, J., & Mohammadi, M. (2019). The Effect of Critical Discourse-Based Instruction on Iranian English Major Students’ Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 33-52. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Fairclough's three-dimensional model of critical discourse analysis as a framework for in-depth reading instruction
description: The article organizes its intervention around Fairclough's three-dimensional model of critical discourse analysis, in which "CDA approach focuses on three dimensions of discourse": text, discourse practice, and socio-cultural practice. These dimensions are analyzed at three levels — description, interpretation, and explanation — and the model treats language as a form of social practice in which ideology is invested in linguistic features. The study operationalized the description level through the ten-question model and had students interpret and explain texts' ideological meanings.
requirements: An experienced teacher familiar with CDA principles to guide interpretation and explanation stages
constraints: The article reports that interpretation and explanation stages "encountered many problems" because students had little acquaintance with macro-level CDA concepts
target_learners: undergraduate EFL English-major students (TEFL, Translation, Literature)
target_learning_goals: critical reading and analysis of implicit and ideological meanings in texts
reading comprehension of ideologically loaded texts
examples: Experimental groups analyzed Inside Reading 3 units and two presidential acceptance speeches using the model's description, interpretation, and explanation levels

article_title: The Effect of Critical Discourse-Based Instruction on Iranian English Major Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Javadi, J., & Mohammadi, M. (2019). The Effect of Critical Discourse-Based Instruction on Iranian English Major Students’ Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 33-52. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Fairclough's ten-question model for text analysis at the description level
description: The ten-question model is a list of "ten main questions and a number of sub-questions" presented by Fairclough (1996) for analyzing texts at the description level to reveal covered meaning. It works on three levels pertaining to vocabulary, grammar, and textual structures, and relies on understanding experiential, relational, and expressive values of linguistic features. In this study it served as the basic device of the CDA-based reading approach, applied by experimental students to course texts and political speeches.
requirements: Learners need prior acquaintance with traditional text analysis, which the article says made the description level "fairly easy" to apply
constraints: The article reports some concepts, such as the classification scheme, were relatively difficult for students, and recommends the model be simplified by experts
target_learning_goals: revealing covered and ideological meanings in texts through vocabulary, grammar, and textual-structure analysis
examples: Students identified hyponyms and synonyms of "terrorism" in Trump's speech, agent-explicit simple sentences, nominalization, inclusive/exclusive pronouns, and foregrounding strategies

article_title: Academic Success Foundation: Enhancing Academic Integrity through Mobile Learning
citation: Alice Schmidt Hanbidge, Amanda Mackenzie, Nicole Sanderson, Kyle Scholz and Tony Tin. (2017). Academic Success Foundation: Enhancing Academic Integrity through Mobile Learning. 13th International Conference Mobile Learning 2017. https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/978-989-8533-61-6
title: Foundations for Academic Success (FAS) mobile learning application for academic integrity
description: The FAS tool is a proposed mobile application delivering academic integrity content through six interactive modules, built on the ProProfs web-based quiz service. It is designed to make information available at students' convenience and thereby acculturate them to university values before classes begin. The article states the tool will "track module completion, but also has capacity to recognize effort and completion by issuing badges and e-certificates". Once completed, the application will be freely accessible for adoption by interested institutions.

Web-based module and assessment delivery via ProProfs
constraints: Designed for the Canadian higher education context; the only similar existing mobile application's content is described as not contextualized to that landscape
target_learners: First to fifth year undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity values: honesty, trust, respect, responsibility, fairness and courage
examples: Modules will be translated into Chinese and piloted by Test Group C; passing a module earns an e-certificate demonstrating AI competency
key_sources: Alice Schmidt Hanbidge, Amanda Mackenzie, Nicole Sanderson, Kyle Scholz and Tony Tin. (2017). Academic Success Foundation: Enhancing Academic Integrity through Mobile Learning. 13th International Conference Mobile Learning 2017. https://isbnsearch.org/isbn/978-989-8533-61-6

requirements: Content review by a focus group before prototype piloting
Quizzes and a final test to certify competency

target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying academic integrity values and rules
examples: Scenarios depict cultural differences, peer pressure and time constraints in student life

article_title: Meaningful Engagement in Facebook Learning Environments: Merging Social and Academic Lives
citation: Wang, J., Lin, C.-F. C., Yu, W.-C. W., & Wu, E. (2013). Meaningful engagement in Facebook learning environments: Merging social and academic lives. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 14(1), Article 26. https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr/
title: Integrate Facebook into instruction following the seven Chickering and Gamson principles to foster engagement
description: The article maps its Facebook instructional practices onto the seven principles for improving undergraduate education (Chickering & Gamson, 1987), arguing that "this study provides support for the 7 principles of good practices of improving engagement in undergraduate education (Chickering and Gamson, 1987) along with the Facebook platform". Facebook features extend communication, support collaborative projects, enable prompt feedback, and maximize time on task.
requirements: Instructors should demonstrate a positive perspective toward Facebook and provide clear instructions and guidelines of Facebook participation, as the article states
constraints: The article cautions that positive results may not be solely attributable to the technology, and that instructors' skills and personal characteristics may be the major cause for increasing student grades and learning engagement

academic grades
student-instructor and student-student relationships

article_title: Vocabulary Learning on Learner-Created Content by Using Web 2.0 Tools
citation: Omer Eren. (2015). Vocabulary Learning on Learner-Created Content by Using Web 2.0 Tools. Contemporary Educational Technology, 6(4), 281-300. https://www.cedtech.net
title: Facebook virtual classroom with four learner-created content assignments
description: The treatment was a closed Facebook group acting as a virtual classroom in which groups of four students created and shared content about assigned vocabulary. The wall feature let members "share their presentations, videos, photos and other documents" and comment on each other's posts. Four assignments structured the twelve-week treatment: Facebook presentations, blog e-portfolios, vocabulary exercises with quizzes, and creating or editing Wikipedia, Wikitravel and Wikihow entries.
requirements: A researcher-created closed Facebook group enrolling all students
Groups of four assigned ten vocabularies per week
An agenda covering the expected 500 vocabularies in three months
constraints: Membership was initially voluntary; only 16 of 23 students joined at first
Mother-tongue (Turkish) commenting caused arguments and needed prohibiting
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge at recognition level
examples: Students prepared PowerPoint presentations with pictures, songs and video clips from YouTube, wrote blog stories containing target words, and created multiple-choice and sentence-completion quizzes

creativity in producing missionary motto

citation: Khaghaninejad, M. S. (2014). Introducing intertextuality-aware instruction as a novel approach of teaching reading passages in EFL context. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 18(1), 65-83. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075042
title: Fairclough's framework of intertextuality types and reporting modes as an analytical model for reading passages
description: The article adopts Fairclough's (1992) critical-discourse-analysis model, which distinguishes "manifest intertextuality" from "interdiscursivity or constitutive intertextuality", plus sequential, embedded, and mixed types, and four reporting modes (direct, indirect, free indirect, narrative report of speech act). The study operationalizes the model to classify vocabulary, structures, genres, reporting modes, and intertextuality types in ten reading passages and to structure the experimental instruction.
requirements: Analysts must trace which texts and voices are included or excluded in a passage, following Fairclough's suggestions as the article states
constraints: The framework was applied only to ten randomly selected passages from one reading-based course-book series
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
critical awareness of textual voices and intertextuality
examples: The article analyzes a passage titled "Zorro: A Review", identifying free indirect reporting and narrative report of speech act in the writer's references to Allende's book and McCully's "The Curse of Capistrano"

article_title: FamuPlus - a pilot project to support self-oriented learning through self-created learning outcomes in clinical electives.
citation: Punz A, Breakell T, Kühlein T, Harendza S, Kunisch R, Engel B. (2026). FamuPlus – a pilot project to support self-oriented learning through self-created learning outcomes in clinical electives. GMS Journal for Medical Education 43(6), Doc76. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume43/zma001870
title: FamuPlus: a four-step pilot program supporting self-created learning outcomes in clinical electives
description: FamuPlus is a pilot project at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg supporting self-oriented learning during clinical electives. Fourteen students participated: seven completed a brief online training on the SMART framework and Bloom's taxonomy, formulated individual learning outcomes, reviewed them with clinical teachers, and completed weekly online self-evaluations on a visual scale from zero to a hundred percent, plus mid-elective interviews and end-of-elective focus groups. Seven control students completed electives without the project. The seven intervention participants formulated 29 learning outcomes, of which 18 related to psychomotor skills, six to cognitive knowledge, and five to affective attitudes.
requirements: Participation was voluntary and students formulated outcomes within a guided process including online training, a digital SMART template, and teacher discussion
constraints: The small, potentially highly motivated cohort limits generalizability; the intervention's components were not evaluated separately
target_learners: medical students in the clinical study phase (third to fifth year)
target_learning_goals: self-oriented learning
goal formulation and reflection during clinical electives
examples: Seven intervention students formulated 29 individual learning outcomes ranging from three to five per student before their month-long electives

article_title: Household income and academic performance in Korean adolescents: A longitudinal test of dual investment pathways.
citation: Kang Ran. (2026). Household income and academic performance in Korean adolescents: A longitudinal test of dual investment pathways. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353476
title: Family Investment Model dual-pathway framework applied to later childhood in Korea
description: The Family Investment Model (FIM) conceptualizes household income as a foundational resource parents convert into two analytically distinct investment pathways: material investments such as educational expenditures, and relational investments such as supportive parent–child interactions. The article states that "the Family Investment Model assumes that family income influences children's developmental outcomes through two analytically distinct yet complementary pathways—material and relational investments." This study extends FIM to later elementary childhood in Korea, testing whether the dual-pathway structure holds in a context of highly institutionalized private education.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-wave data with baseline controls on both mediators and outcome to draw temporal inferences about pathway-specific effects
constraints: The article notes most foundational FIM research emphasizes early childhood, and pathway strength may vary across developmental periods or sociocultural environments
target_learners: Korean early adolescents in the later elementary years (Grade 4 cohort)
target_learning_goals: Academic performance as shaped by family economic resources and investment processes

description: The article recommends that implementation of the ICO-OCEX 'should be accompanied by faculty orientation to ensure consistent application.' Faculty attended a structured virtual orientation covering the framework, behavioral descriptors, sample rating demonstrations, and common rater errors. The authors note that 'Structured faculty development and calibration workshops may further reduce rating variability and improve scoring consistency.'

article_title: Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on math performance?
citation: Miller‐Cotto, D., & Medrano, J. (2026). Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on math performance? British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 108–126. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12781
title: Faded worked examples: sequentially removing problem steps across a problem set until the learner solves independently
description: This pattern structures a practice set so that assistance is gradually withdrawn: in faded worked examples, "steps are removed sequentially from the worked examples for the learner to complete until they solve the problem independently." In this study's implementation, across six problems per session the number of removed steps increased from one (the answer) in the first problem to the full problem prompt in the sixth, in backward-fading fashion. It was delivered as online homework on geometry problems in ASSISTments.
requirements: A sequence of problems of the same type so that removed steps can progress from one step to the entire problem across the set
constraints: In this study the fading schedule meant steps across conditions were not constant, which the authors flag as a possible dosage issue, though their dosage test found no evidence for it
target_learning_goals: geometry problem solving: surface area and volume of three-dimensional shapes
examples: Across three homework sessions, fading-condition students completed six problems per session in which one, then two, then up to all steps were removed, ending with only the problem prompt

article_title: Changing perspectives: The development of preservice teachers' field-specific ability beliefs across academic disciplines.
citation: Asbury, K., Carstensen, B., & Klusmann, U. (2026). Changing perspectives: The development of preservice teachers' field‐specific ability beliefs across academic disciplines. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 337–355. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70019
title: Field‐specific ability beliefs (FABs) as a field‐specific, socially embedded construct distinct from general mindsets
description: Field‐specific ability beliefs reflect "the perception that success in academic fields depends on innate, unteachable abilities" (Leslie et al., 2015). The article distinguishes FABs from Dweck's mindset theory: mindsets are domain‐general and self‐focused beliefs about one's own ability malleability, whereas FABs are "socially shared perceptions about what it takes to succeed in specific academic fields." Empirical studies confirm the two are distinct constructs. FABs are embedded in the COACTIV model of teacher professional competence as a component of teacher beliefs that shape instructional practices and student outcomes.
requirements: Measured with a validated three‐item scale (Leslie et al., 2015; German adaptation by Heyder et al., 2020) on a seven‐point scale, with demonstrated internal consistency (.80 < α < .85) and longitudinal measurement invariance
constraints: Scalar invariance was not consistently established across academic disciplines, particularly at the study's beginning and end, which may affect comparability of mean FAB scores between fields
target_learning_goals: understanding beliefs about the role of innate ability in academic success across disciplines

constraints: The article states directionality cannot be inferred due to cross-sectional data, so results are exploratory.
target_learning_goals: STEM achievement (science and mathematics GPA)
spatial thinking

article_title: Challenges in student assessment in medical and health sciences education in Northern Iraq.
citation: Aziz Shahram, Hameed Masood, Azeez Shokhan, Omer Shirwan, Ameen Kawa, Abdullah Trefa, Nada Mohanad. (2025). Challenges in student assessment in medical and health sciences education in Northern Iraq. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07643-4
title: Institutions should recognize student failure as an essential part of education and professional growth rather than a reflection of institutional shortcomings
description: The article argues that institutions and faculty should reframe student failure as a normal, constructive element of education rather than an institutional shortcoming, because treating failure as taboo makes educators reluctant to fail underperforming students and reinforces grading leniency. Recommended mechanisms include "Public awareness campaigns and workshops" stressing that fair assessment practices promote both student growth and patient safety.
requirements: Public awareness campaigns and workshops to change the cultural perception of failure, stressing that fair assessment promotes student growth and patient safety
target_learners: medical and health sciences educators in Iraq
institutional leaders in Iraqi higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate competency-based assessment of students
student growth through constructive handling of failure
examples: In the survey, 39% of educators saw failing a student as a last resort and only 11% considered it a necessary part of education, and only 19.9% felt confident after making a fail decision.

title: Faculty should shape students' academic identity and foster positive excitement through supportive interactions
description: The article assigns faculty a pivotal role: their capacity "can be leveraged to shape and strengthen students' academic identity," and they should create learning environments fostering positive excitement and use students' emotions to facilitate learning. It recommends making the most of supportive opportunities, "even the smallest and seemingly insignificant gestures (such as a simple smile)," to foster growth and engagement, since supportive interactions inspire hope and more enthusiastic engagement in studies.

Academic performance
examples: The article recommends faculty leverage supportive interactions such as a simple smile, based on its findings that identity, emotions, and enthusiasm predict performance

title: Fair Grader 2000 digital teaching practice evaluation system for objective post-hoc cavity preparation scoring
description: Fair Grader 2000 (NISSIN, Japan) is a standardized digital evaluation system for dental cavity preparation. The article describes it as combining "scanning and 3D imaging technology", using a non-contact 3D scan of the tooth preparation to score cavity morphology, cutting volume and volume ratio against a standard model, with a maximum score of 100 points. Unlike real-time systems it cannot provide feedback during preparation, but it requires no special instruments, can be sent for assessment post-operation, and was used here for baseline and final scoring of faculty competence.

constraints: Cannot provide real-time feedback and guidance during the cavity preparation process, unlike the Aizhixing system

dental students in preclinical simulation courses
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of cavity preparation quality
examples: Used to establish baseline scores before Aizhixing training and final scores after the fourth examination cycle

article_title: Turning nursing students' mistakes into resources for learning in simulation-based training: facilitators' assumptions about providing feedback in debriefing.
citation: Lervik W, Solberg M, Wiig AC, Berg H. (2025). Turning nursing students' mistakes into resources for learning in simulation-based training: facilitators' assumptions about providing feedback in debriefing. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06628-z
title: Facilitators' assumptions about learning shape how students' mistakes are used as learning resources in debriefing
description: The study's organizing account is that facilitators' fundamental assumptions about learning — about safety, positive feedback, students' self-awareness, and what counts as a mistake — determine how they use mistakes as learning opportunities during debriefing. The authors conclude that "facilitators' assumptions about learning affect how they use students' mistakes as learning opportunities". The account frames simulation debriefing as an ambiguous and complex praxis in which facilitators balance preserving safety and mastery against addressing performance gaps.
requirements: Facilitators responsible for raising students' awareness of performances and facilitating reflection during debriefing
constraints: Based on interviews with nine experienced facilitators in Norway; the authors call for future research on authentic debriefing interactions
target_learning_goals: reflection on performance gaps
learning from mistakes
professional nursing procedures
examples: Four themes from thematic analysis: conceptions of mistakes, fostering positivity, creating a safe space, and variable approaches to addressing mistakes

title: FateSim extracurricular FATE workshop with the Vimedix ultrasound simulator
description: A FATE-specific workshop taught to third-year medical students, built on a WINFOCUS-based FOCUS training concept, comparing training on the "validated ultrasound simulator (Vimedix, CAE Healthcare, Sarasota, Florida, US), approved by experts" with traditional training on live human subjects. The course comprised an introductory plenary session, practical exercises rotating through three stations per modality with four students per peer-tutor station, and DOPS practical tests on both simulator and humans. Ten didactically trained peer tutors taught under supervision of two consultants.

title: Prepare and support facilitators with relevant training, prebriefs, and post-workshop debriefs when teaching sensitive DEI content
description: Because challenging questions and discussions arose in every workshop, the authors found facilitator selection and preparation central: it is "helpful for facilitators to engage in relationship-centered communication training, trauma-informed care training, and de-escalation training." They also recommend co-facilitation with varied skill sets, rehearsing facilitation with contingency plans in a prebrief, and consistent facilitators across sessions to build rapport and relational trust, with facilitators debriefing among themselves after each workshop.

constraints: Facilitators with less DEI training experience are advised to take relevant courses before leading
target_learners: Faculty facilitators of DEI and microaggression workshops
target_learning_goals: Safe, well-facilitated practice of microaggression response skills
examples: Two facilitators in the pilot had formal training in trauma-informed care and de-escalation techniques.

title: Family Management Style Framework (FMSF)
description: The article defines FMSF as "the entire family working as a team to organize, integrate, and accomplish the tasks associated to condition management of children with chronic illnesses". It frames family management as a long-term process in which parents follow a management plan to provide home care after discharge. In the study, FMSF grounded both the routine-care control condition and the FaMM outcome measure, and prior evidence cited links it to adherence and health outcomes in pediatric rheumatism and asthma.

Health education materials such as a family management manual
constraints: The article notes family management may not show good outcomes for families who fail to fully comply, since researchers cannot monitor families' behaviors and skills all the time
target_learners: Families of children with chronic illnesses
target_learning_goals: Organizing and integrating condition-management tasks across the family
Sustained home care after discharge
examples: The control group received FMSF: multidisciplinary assessment, family task assignment, health education, medication guides, and biweekly follow-up after discharge

article_title: Simulation in neonatal care: towards a change in traditional training?
citation: Yousef Nadya, Moreau Romain, Soghier Lamia. (2022). Simulation in neonatal care: towards a change in traditional training? European Journal of Pediatrics 181:1429–1436. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04373-3
title: Post-simulation debriefing with facilitator-guided reflective models as a core component of simulation-based education
description: The review frames post-simulation debriefing as "one of the most important components of simulation-based education and is critical to the learning experience". Its objective is to encourage learners' reflective thinking and provide feedback about performance, letting learners reformulate the experienced scenario, explain thought processes, discuss mistakes, and identify unmet needs. Facilitator-guided debriefing is the most common and most extensively studied method, and models such as advocacy inquiry, PEARLS, and plus-delta all focus on deep self-driven learner reflection on action as described by Kolb.
requirements: A teaching plan including learning objectives is essential to scenario design and debriefing
constraints: There is currently no evidence for the best method for debriefing
target_learners: Neonatal care clinicians and trainees in NICU settings
target_learning_goals: Reflective learning from simulated performance, non-technical skills, and achievement of scenario learning objectives
examples: Facilitator-guided debriefing ensures learners realize all scenario learning objectives and internalize triumphs and failures through their own reflection.

article_title: It's All in the Family: Parents' Economic Worries and Youth's Perceptions of Financial Stress and Educational Outcomes.
citation: Mistry, R. S., & Elenbaas, L. (2021). It’s All in the Family: Parents’ Economic Worries and Youth’s Perceptions of Financial Stress and Educational Outcomes. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-021-01393-4
title: Family Economic Stress Model applied to preadolescents' academic adjustment
description: The family economic stress perspective posits that "family experiences of financial strain due, for example, to unstable work, low income, or income loss, causes parents to worry about their finances" and, in turn, emotional distress that interferes with couple relationships and parenting. A central tenet is that "people’s perceptions of how they are doing financially (i.e., economic pressure) have a downstream influence on family functioning" over and above SES. This study extends the model to preadolescents' perceptions and academic outcomes in middle- to higher-SES families.
requirements: Measures distinguishing perceived economic stress about needs from wants, and SSS ladder ratings, for both parents and youth
constraints: Most supporting research cited focuses on families experiencing job loss, financial instability, or poverty; this study's evidence comes from a cross-sectional, mostly middle- to higher-SES sample
target_learners: Preadolescent and early adolescent youth ages 8–14 and their parents
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement, academic motivation, and expectations for educational attainment
examples: The study tested the model with SEM path analyses linking income, parent and youth needs/wants stress, SSS, and three academic outcomes

article_title: HipSim - hip fracture surgery simulation utilizing the Learning Curve-Cumulative Summation test (LC-CUSUM).
citation: Rölfing Jan Duedal, Jensen Rune Dall, Paltved Charlotte. (2020). HipSim — hip fracture surgery simulation utilizing the Learning Curve–Cumulative Summation test (LC-CUSUM). Acta Orthopaedica 91(6): 669–674. https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2020.1777511
title: Use LC-CUSUM pass/fail results in formative simulation to guide educator attention: reassure on passing, trigger career counselling and close supervision on failing
description: The authors recommend that LC-CUSUM pass/fail results direct educator attention in formative simulation programs: 'failing HipSim should raise concerns and career counselling and close clinical supervision seem to be appropriate measures', while passing may reassure clinical supervisors of a resident's potential. The recommendation rests on the observed association between passing HipSim and continuing a career in orthopedics.
requirements: An LC-CUSUM-based pass/fail assessment of each simulation must be in place within the formative simulation program.
Educators must have access to participants' pass/fail status early in the 1st year of residency.
constraints: The article states 'Passing HipSim may be a confounder for the determination of the participant to become an orthopedic surgeon'.
The article states these hypotheses 'require further scientific investigations', and that some junior doctors in other specialties did not return for the second training day.
target_learning_goals: career decision-making in orthopedic surgery
safe progression to supervised clinical practice
examples: 9/18 participants failing HipSim in their 1st year did not continue in orthopedics; the authors suggest failing should draw educators' attention to career counselling for first-year residents.

article_title: The Effect of Passive and Active Education Methods Applied in Repetition Activities on the Retention of Anatomical Knowledge.

title: Facilitate retrieval of earlier learned knowledge at the right position in a spiral curriculum, in any format
description: The article recommends that curricula deliberately schedule revisits of previously learned knowledge, because any rehearsing act improved long-term retention regardless of format. As the authors conclude, "If durable education in a spiral curriculum is strived for, teachers should be aware to facilitate the retrieval of earlier learned knowledge at the right position in the curriculum." The repetition format "could be a multiple‐choice test, a traditional lecture in a massive hall, collaborative small group work, or an e‐learning module."
requirements: A repetition activity or test must revisit previously learned knowledge at a suitable point in the curriculum or learning path
constraints: The study tested only repetition activities already integrated at Nijmegen; game-based or drawing-based activities were not considered
Repetition content must not be revisited in other courses during the measurement period for effects to be attributable
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of anatomical (basic science) knowledge
examples: Groups 3–5 attended a 1.5-hour lecture, e-learning module, or small-group dissection-room session 14 weeks after the Functional Anatomy course, with the same study material in all three activities
